study_notes.topic: Quantity Comparison (Q1 vs Q2) - Quantitative Aptitude

sections.title: Advanced Concept: Inequalities, Variables, and Complex Arithmetic
sections.content: Level 3 questions involve deep algebraic inequalities, advanced mensuration (3D geometry), permutations & combinations, and probability. Here, one or both quantities might not yield a single number, but a range of possible values.

sections.title: Handling Variables and Inequality Ranges
sections.content: If Q1 or Q2 results in a variable range (e.g., Q1 = x where 5 < x < 10, and Q2 = 7), you must test the boundary conditions. If x can be 6 (Q1 < Q2) and x can be 9 (Q1 > Q2), the relationship Cannot Be Determined (CND).

sections.title: Mensuration Constant Cancellation
sections.content: When comparing areas or volumes (e.g., Cylinder vs Cone), do not calculate the value of π (22/7). Leave all constants (π, √3, fractions) intact. Cancel out common factors from Q1 and Q2 to compare the residual multipliers.

sections.title: Probability and Combinatorics
sections.content: These chapters naturally fit Q1/Q2. Q1 might be the probability of drawing 2 red balls, Q2 the probability of drawing 2 blue balls. If the total number of balls is the same, just compare the numerators (the combinations of drawing the colors). The denominators (total outcomes) are identical and can be ignored.

sections.title: The 'Data Sufficiency' Overlap
sections.content: Sometimes Q1/Q2 questions act like Data Sufficiency. If Q1 lacks enough data to find a specific value or range, and Q2 is a fixed number, the relationship is automatically CND.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Multiplying by π (3.14) in Mensuration comparisons, wasting minutes. 2. Forgetting that variables can be negative or fractions between 0 and 1 when dealing with inequalities. 3. Calculating the full denominator in probability when both quantities share the same sample space.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 3 requires strategic laziness. Cancel out common constants, ignore identical denominators, and vigorously test the extreme limits (boundaries) of variable ranges to quickly expose CND scenarios.

short_tricks.topic: Quantity Comparison (Q1 vs Q2) - Quantitative Aptitude

tricks.title: The Constant Cancellation Trick
tricks.explanation: In 3D Mensuration, never expand constants. If comparing the volume of a sphere (Q1) and a cylinder (Q2), drop the π immediately from both sides before calculating.
tricks.example: Q1: Volume of sphere radius 3 = (4/3)*π*27 = 36π. Q2: Volume of cylinder radius 3, height 5 = π*9*5 = 45π. Cancel π. 36 < 45. Q1 < Q2.

tricks.title: Denominator Match in Probability
tricks.explanation: If Q1 and Q2 draw from the same bag or deck of cards, the total possible outcomes (denominator) are exactly the same. Just calculate and compare the favorable outcomes (numerators).
tricks.example: Bag has 5 Red, 4 Blue. Q1: Prob of 2 Red = 5C2 = 10. Q2: Prob of 2 Blue = 4C2 = 6. Denominator is 9C2 for both. 10 > 6, so Q1 > Q2.

tricks.title: Boundary Testing (Extremes)
tricks.explanation: If Q1 = 'Value of x where 2x - 4 > 10' (so x > 7). Q2 = 10. Test a number close to the boundary (x=8) and a large extreme (x=100).
tricks.example: If x=8, Q1 < Q2. If x=15, Q1 > Q2. Since the signs flip depending on the value chosen within the valid range, mark CND instantly.

tricks.title: The Fractional Base Trap
tricks.explanation: If Q1 = x² and Q2 = x³, and you are told x > 0. Do not automatically assume Q2 > Q1. If x is a fraction between 0 and 1 (e.g., 1/2), x² is 1/4 and x³ is 1/8. Here, Q1 > Q2. Always test fractions.
